# Optical-property assembly and spectral integration {#sec-ch07}

A radiation band first combines opacity sources into one set of layer properties, then solves radiative transfer
at each spectral point. The final sum must use the same spectral measure as those solver outputs.

@sec-ch07-mixture derives the scattering-weighted mixture and its conservative-scattering cap.
@sec-ch07-spectral distinguishes spectral densities from interval-integrated fluxes and documents their accumulation.
The evidence separates native measurements already recorded from the record and algebra checks run for this manuscript.

## Combining optical properties (`opacities`) {#sec-ch07-mixture}

<!-- PROVENANCE
pin: pyharp@f34506f9d14ee7b1f2e1222775baa5093ae6967f
sources: src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp; src/opacity/scattering_functions.cpp

### Summary

Several absorbers and scatterers can occupy the same layer. The band adds their extinction but averages their phase
functions using scattering strength, so a purely absorbing source cannot change the angular distribution of scattering.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Construct the mixture in @eq-ch07-mixture-average.

**Data.** Extinction in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, dimensionless albedo and moments, thickness in $\mathrm{m}$.

**Placement.** Before the selected transfer solver, independently at each spectral point and layer.

**Activation.** Always for the band's `opacities`[^rg-d31dbcab05aa]; there is no mixture switch.

**Guarantee / limits.** Nonnegative physical inputs; the albedo cap perturbs conservative scattering.

**Evidence.** Stored native results and their record audit appear in the Tests layer.
:::

Local symbols are the source index $a$, extinction $k_a$, scattering $s_a$ and absorption $a_a$, all in
$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; the single-scattering albedo $\omega_a$ and moments $\chi_{a,l}$ are dimensionless.
The Legendre degree is $l$, scattering angle cosine is $x$, and the normalized phase function is $P_a(x)$.
The geometric layer thickness is $\Delta z$ in $\mathrm{m}$ and its optical thickness is $\Delta\tau$.
The positive cap distance is $\delta\omega$, distinct from relative error $\epsilon$.

### Derivation

Assume each source provides nonnegative extinction and an albedo between zero and one. Split extinction into
scattering and absorption before adding sources:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_a &= k_a\omega_a,\\
a_a &= k_a(1-\omega_a),\\
k &= \sum_a(a_a+s_a)=\sum_a k_a,\\
s &= \sum_a s_a.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-mixture-sums}

`RadiationBandImpl::forward` evaluates the extinction and scattering sums in @eq-ch07-mixture-sums
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
The absorption split explains the sum; the implementation adds extinction directly.

Normalize the phase function so that half its integral over angle cosine equals one. Its moments and expansion are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi_{a,l} &= \frac12\int_{-1}^{1}P_l(x)P_a(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
P_a(x) &= \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(2l+1)\chi_{a,l}P_l(x),\\
\chi_{a,0} &= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial. The definition is unnumbered after Eq. (6d) on p. 2503 of
@reading01. The Fourier scattering kernel is Eq. (6b), not Eq. (14) or (15).
Those latter equations on p. 2505 expand bottom bidirectional reflectivity in surface moments.
There is no Eq. (6e) in that sequence.

For positive total scattering, conservation of the scattered source requires $sP=\sum_a s_aP_a$.
Multiply this equality by $P_l/2$, integrate and substitute the moment definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s\chi_l &= \sum_a s_a\frac12\int_{-1}^{1}P_l(x)P_a(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\\
s\chi_l &= \sum_a s_a\chi_{a,l},\\
\chi_l &= \frac{\sum_a s_a\chi_{a,l}}{s},\\
\omega &= \frac{s}{k}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-mixture-average}

`RadiationBandImpl::forward` implements @eq-ch07-mixture-average
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
This scattering weighting agrees with Eq. (8) of @reading12.
If a denominator is nonpositive, `divide_where_positive` returns zero
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp divide_where_positive repo=pyharp >}}).
For physical inputs this defines the vacuum albedo and zero-scattering moments without dividing by zero.

Assume extinction is constant within a layer. Integrating along the geometric thickness gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\tau &= \int_{z_{\mathrm{bot}}}^{z_{\mathrm{top}}}k\,\mathrm{d}z,\\
\Delta\tau &= k\Delta z,\\
\omega^{\mathrm{solver}} &= \min(\omega,1-\delta\omega).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-mixture-cap}

`RadiationBandImpl::forward` implements @eq-ch07-mixture-cap with $\delta\omega=10^{-12}$ for float64 and
$10^{-6}$ otherwise ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
The source documents this as regularization of conservative-scattering degeneracies. It changes the solver's
albedo, not the original sources, optical thickness or moments. It is not delta-Eddington rescaling.

For positive extinction and scattering, the mixture identities are exact before floating-point rounding.
Finite stored moment arrays truncate the angular representation; the resulting flux error is not measured here.
The cap changes the albedo by at most $\delta\omega$ for physical inputs.
The exact worked mixture and Rayleigh normalization are checked by `ch07_evidence_check.py`, line `[C7]`.

### Numerical method

The property tensor has shape `(nwave,ncol,nlyr,nprop)`. Each entry belongs to a layer, not a face.
Assembly is an explicit reduction over opacity sources with no iteration or boundary solve.
The method clears the destination, adds extinction and scattering numerators, normalizes, multiplies by thickness,
and caps albedo before calling the solver. @fig-ch07-mixture-flow shows this order.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
![Mixture data flow. Blue boxes hold source coefficients; green boxes form layer properties; the orange box receives the capped solver input. Arrows give evaluation order.](07-assembly_files/figure-pdf/fig-ch07-mixture-flow-output-1.pdf){#fig-ch07-mixture-flow fig-alt='Sources feed sums, normalization, thickness conversion and an albedo cap, then the transfer solver.'}
:::
:::


The stored moments start at degree one. `henyey_greenstein` supplies Henyey-Greenstein powers of the asymmetry
parameter ({{< code src/opacity/scattering_functions.cpp henyey_greenstein repo=pyharp >}}).
The DISORT adapter inserts the normalized degree-zero moment before copying higher moments
({{< code src/disort_impl.h repo=pydisort >}}).
A missing higher moment contributes zero to its numerator while that source still contributes scattering to the denominator.
This padding convention does not prove the physical moment vanishes.

: Mixture implementation map. {#tbl-ch07-mixture-code}

To use the mixture, list the selected opacity names in the band's `opacities`. The sources return extinction,
albedo when present, and moments when present. An extinction-only source is purely absorbing.
The following excerpt maps the accumulation to @eq-ch07-mixture-sums and @eq-ch07-mixture-average;
`IEX`, `ISS` and `IPM` are the extinction, scattering and first-moment slots:

```cpp
prop.select(-1, disort::IEX) += kdata.select(-1, disort::IEX);
prop.select(-1, disort::ISS) +=
    kdata.select(-1, disort::ISS) * kdata.select(-1, disort::IEX);
```

The excerpt is from `RadiationBandImpl::forward`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
That function checks the layer and column counts against `conc`, `dz` and options, and checks the spectral count.
Thickness may have shape `(nlyr)` or `(ncol,nlyr)`. With `verbose` enabled it prints each accumulation stage.
It does not impose the physical nonnegativity assumptions used in this derivation.

The native record contains 78 passing cases, 506 scalar comparisons and six passing metamorphic checks.
They cover source reversal, splitting and batch-versus-cell evaluation in both precisions.[^ch07-assembly-run]
The largest relative errors are below $4\,10^{-16}$ in float64 and $2.4\,10^{-7}$ in float32.
These are round-off observations, judged against the stated tolerances, not portable last digits.[^ch07-assembly-run]
The tolerances allow more than one hundred unit round-offs for the short reduction and division chains.
Tiny nonzero references additionally require relative agreement; an absolute threshold alone would hide their loss.

For sources $(k,\omega,g)=(2,0.5,0.6)$ and $(3,0.8,-0.2)$, plus pure absorption $5\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$,

### Limits

The capture solver returns zero flux; this experiment validates the properties supplied to a solver, not physical fluxes.
The test-only property-buffer setup does not validate production allocation policy.
CUDA, gradients, half precision, negative inputs, real opacity tables and a systematic subnormal campaign are not measured.
The cap's effect on flux or heating is not measured. The test does not independently demonstrate the degeneracy cited
in the source comment. Spectral accumulation has separate limitations in @sec-ch07-spectral.

## Matching the spectral measure (`weight` or `wavenumber`) {#sec-ch07-spectral}

<!-- PROVENANCE
pin: pyharp@f34506f9d14ee7b1f2e1222775baa5093ae6967f
sources: src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp; src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp; src/radiation/bbflux.cpp
status: draft
-->

### Summary

A solver output can represent either flux per unit wavenumber or flux already integrated across an interval.
The final accumulator must distinguish them. Integrating an interval flux over wavenumber again introduces an extra
spectral-width factor, even when the transfer solution itself is accurate.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Match the source measure to @eq-ch07-spectral-trapezoid or @eq-ch07-spectral-weight.

**Data.** Wavenumber in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; integrated flux in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.

**Placement.** After each spectral transfer solve, before the band's flux is returned.

**Activation.** Nonempty `weight` selects a sum; otherwise `wavenumber` selects a trapezoid.

**Guarantee / limits.** No automatic check that source and accumulator units agree.

**Evidence.** Stored thermal controls and their audit appear in the Tests layer.
:::

Local symbols are wavenumber $\nu$ in $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, spectral index $j$, interval endpoints
$\nu_{\mathrm{lo}}$ and $\nu_{\mathrm{hi}}$, and width $\Delta\nu=\nu_{\mathrm{hi}}-\nu_{\mathrm{lo}}$.
The spectral radiance $B_\nu(T)$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}\,(cm^{-1})^{-1}}$;
$\mathcal B(T)$ is its interval integral in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$.
The density $F_\nu$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,(cm^{-1})^{-1}}$;
$\mathcal F_j$ is a point's interval-integrated solver output in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$.
Quadrature weights $w_j$ and absorption rank $\eta$ are dimensionless.
The asymmetry parameter $g$ retains its angular meaning in @sec-ch07-mixture.

### Derivation

For thermal emission the source in the transfer equation is monochromatic: $(1-\omega)B_\nu(T)$.
This is Eq. (2) on p. 16289 of @reading02 and Eq. (3) on p. 2503 of @reading01.
Their spectral variable is frequency; the implementation uses wavenumber and the corresponding transformed density.
An interval-integrated radiance is

$$
\mathcal B(T)=\int_{\nu_{\mathrm{lo}}}^{\nu_{\mathrm{hi}}}B_\nu(T)\,\mathrm{d}\nu.
$$ {#eq-ch07-spectral-planck}

`bbflux_wavenumber` evaluates @eq-ch07-spectral-planck for unequal endpoints on the Toon path
({{< code src/radiation/bbflux.cpp bbflux_wavenumber overload=3 repo=pyharp >}}).
For DISORT, `c_planck_func2` documents the same interval contract and a density branch for equal endpoints
({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_planck_func2 repo=pydisort >}}).
The paper's monochromatic convention does not make these interval outputs spectral densities.

Suppose the transfer output is a density. Linearly interpolate it over each increasing grid interval and integrate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_\nu(\nu) &\simeq F_{\nu,j}
 +\frac{\nu-\nu_j}{\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j}(F_{\nu,j+1}-F_{\nu,j}),\\
\int_{\nu_j}^{\nu_{j+1}} F_\nu\,\mathrm{d}\nu
 &\simeq (\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j)F_{\nu,j}
 +\frac{\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j}{2}(F_{\nu,j+1}-F_{\nu,j}),\\
F &\simeq \sum_j\frac{\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j}{2}(F_{\nu,j}+F_{\nu,j+1}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-spectral-trapezoid}

`sum_spectrum` selects the trapezoid in @eq-ch07-spectral-trapezoid
({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp sum_spectrum repo=pyharp >}}), implemented by `trapezoid`
({{< code src/math/trapezoid.cpp trapezoid repo=pyharp >}}).
For twice continuously differentiable density, linear-interpolation error on an interval of width $h_j$ is bounded
by $M u(h_j-u)/2$, where $u$ is distance from its left endpoint and $M$ bounds $|F_\nu''|$ on the band.
Integrating this bound and then summing intervals gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
|E_j| &\le \frac{M}{2}\int_0^{h_j}u(h_j-u)\,\mathrm{d}u,\\
|E_j| &\le \frac{M h_j^3}{12},\\
\sum_j |E_j| &\le \frac{M h^2}{12}\sum_j h_j
 =\frac{M h^2\Delta\nu}{12}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $E_j$ is the interval flux error and $h$ is the largest grid width.
This is a quadrature bound, not a measured convergence order for the transfer solver.

Alternatively, represent a normalized absorption-rank integral by quadrature. Under the assumption that the
chosen interval Planck source is appropriate for each term, the matching discrete rule is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 1\,\mathrm{d}\eta &= 1,\\
\sum_j w_j &= 1,\\
F &\simeq \sum_j w_j\mathcal F_j.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-spectral-weight}

`sum_spectrum` computes the final sum in @eq-ch07-spectral-weight
({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp sum_spectrum repo=pyharp >}}); it does not normalize or validate the weights.
Normalization is within each physical band, not across unrelated spectral bins.
The first two lines define the convention tested here; they are not an assertion that every opacity-file weight
has these units. A general correlated-k accuracy analysis is outside this chapter.

For a grey isothermal test, each point receives the same interval-integrated thermal source and returns the same
$\mathcal F$. The normalized sum gives $\mathcal F$. Applying the trapezoid to those same values instead gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{\mathrm{repeated}} &= \sum_j(\nu_{j+1}-\nu_j)\mathcal F,\\
F^{\mathrm{repeated}} &= (\nu_{\mathrm{hi}}-\nu_{\mathrm{lo}})\mathcal F,\\
F^{\mathrm{repeated}} &= \Delta\nu\mathcal F.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch07-spectral-width}

The selection in `RadiationBandImpl::forward` causes @eq-ch07-spectral-width when weights are empty and each point
retains the same band limits ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
The numerical width factor has units $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$; this is a dimensional inconsistency, not a physical flux gain.
Check `[C7]` proves the constant and affine identities exactly; `[C3]` tests the width identity in stored native outputs.

### Numerical method

`RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml` assigns the full band limits to every spectral point for both Toon and DISORT
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml repo=pyharp >}}).
`ToonMcKay89Impl::forward` passes these endpoints to the Planck routine
({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.cpp ToonMcKay89Impl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
Thus the default endpoint setup supplies an interval source, independently of the later accumulator choice.

::: {.cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3}
![Spectral measure choices. The blue branch carries a density and uses a trapezoid; the green branch carries an interval flux and uses dimensionless weights. The red dashed arrow marks the inconsistent extra integration.](07-assembly_files/figure-pdf/fig-ch07-spectral-flow-output-1.pdf){#fig-ch07-spectral-flow fig-alt='A density goes to a wavenumber trapezoid; an interval flux goes to a weighted sum. Sending the interval flux to the trapezoid adds a width factor.'}
:::
:::


Each spectrum has a spectral axis, a column axis, a level axis and a flux-channel axis. The reduction removes only
the spectral axis. The flux channels store nonnegative upward and downward magnitudes; net flux is upward minus
downward in `cal_net_flux` ({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp cal_net_flux repo=pyharp >}}).
Vertical arrays run from bottom to top. The audit uses top upward flux and treats atmosphere and surface temperatures
as separate inputs. Assembly itself has no spectral iteration or convergence criterion.

: Spectral implementation map. {#tbl-ch07-spectral-code}

`bands`[^rg-082ffa154e1b] is the list of radiation-band configurations.
`name`[^rg-11346b87d129] is the band identifier.
`solver` is the transfer-solver selector.
`range`[^rg-593a41923a13] is the pair of spectral endpoints, interpreted as wavenumbers by default.
`nwave`[^rg-d1be40df31ac] is the number of spectral points.
`nstr`[^rg-e099cb0e45b5] is the discrete-ordinate stream count.
`flags`[^rg-82c32909bbf2] is the comma-separated solver options.
`opacities` is the list of opacity-source names used by the band.

The historical test constructs a minimal band through YAML, with a generated grey-opacity file:

```yaml
bands:
  - name: bx
    solver: disort
    range: [600.0, 800.0]
    nwave: 16
    nstr: 4
    flags: lamber,quiet,onlyfl,planck
    opacities: [grey]
```

The complete generated configuration, including species, geometry and opacity registration, is in the committed
`band_lab.py` helper. The helper explicitly assigns `nphase = nstr`; the experiment does not rely on the YAML
path initializing it. After parsing, the three test configurations are:

```python
# Interval flux with normalized weights:
bo.weight([1.0 / nwave] * nwave)
# Existing endpoint setup with wavenumber accumulation:
bo.wavenumber(list(nu))
# Density experiment, in a separately constructed band:
bo.wavenumber(list(nu))
bo.set_wave_lower(list(nu))
bo.set_wave_upper(list(nu))
```

These are alternative configurations, not successive mutations of one band. Nonempty weights take precedence even
if wavenumbers also exist. The density experiment is a diagnostic, not a safe Toon workaround: its equal-endpoint
Planck branch has a separate recorded failure.

`from_yaml` requires `bands`, a matching band name, `opacities`, `nwave`, geometry cells with `nx1`, and a supported
`solver`; `twostr` is rejected. It defaults `nstr` to four and `verbose` to false.
Toon-specific flags and temperature interpolation belong to the solver and API chapters.
At the accumulation boundary, `sum_spectrum` requires a one-dimensional coordinate/weight tensor and rejects unknown
mode names. Neither it nor the band checks the spectral units or requires weights to sum to one.

The thermal control uses one column, eight layers at $250\,\mathrm{K}$, grey absorption with total optical thickness
40, no scattering and a black surface at the same temperature. The exact outgoing blackbody reference is
$\pi\int B_\nu\,\mathrm{d}\nu$, evaluated by independent quadrature with SI defining constants.[^ch07-spectral-run]
Optically thin or reflective boundary variations are ratio controls, not additional blackbody-equilibrium tests.

For DISORT with 128 points, the recorded existing-wavenumber ratios grow from approximately one to ten,
200 and 1000 as the width increases through $1$, $10$, $200$ and $1000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.
Both normalized-weight and density controls remain close to unity, as shown in
@fig-ch07-spectral-ratios.[^ch07-spectral-run]

The width identity holds below $10^{-12}$ relative across 40 grid/solver/width combinations and 24 paired
boundary/solver/opacity variations.[^ch07-spectral-run] Refining the grey grid does not remove the extra width.
The three normalized-bin controls have relative error below $1.1\,10^{-5}$; four Planck tilings agree with
$\sigma T^4$ within $10^{-4}$.[^ch07-spectral-run]

### Limits

The repeated integration is retained as a CANDIDATE defect. No authoritative defect numbering is assigned here.
A density-endpoint change alone is not sufficient for Toon: the equal-endpoint Planck branch needs separate treatment.
The scripts retain the original failures; no solver code is changed.

ReSPQ weight units remain unresolved. `RespqTableImpl` divides file weights by point width
({{< code src/opacity/respq_table.cpp repo=pyharp >}}), whereas `PicasoCKImpl` reads the same variable name without that division
({{< code src/opacity/picaso_ck.cpp repo=pyharp >}}). Width division is consistent with the tested interval-source convention only
if the file weights already carry wavenumber units. No real table from either producer is tested.
The supplied table conventions therefore cannot be inferred from the variable name alone.

The spectral record covers CPU float64, one column, grey or manufactured line absorption, and no scattering.
CUDA, batching, float32, scattering, `area_scale` and the multiband wrapper are not measured.
Surface-albedo behavior differs between the tested solver paths, but its mechanism is not established here.
The blackbody reference must not be extended to arbitrary reflective or nonequilibrium boundaries.

The pydisort wheel reports its release version but no compiled commit. The saved source comparison establishes
identity of its bundled cdisort text, not of its binary. Full source-pin runtime provenance remains open.
The full text of @reading08 was unavailable to the evidence preparation; this chapter does not attribute its
normalization derivation to an unread paper. A complete correlated-k treatment and real-table validation remain open.
